1.point: Open with the Sha'ban prayer, name the two outcomes of annihilation (drunk and sober), and say the chapter will show who stayed drunk, who came back, the theory their heir made, and the critics' concerns with their answers.
steps: Hook: the prayer asks for a place among those who swooned; some reached it
Recall Chapter Twelve in one or two sentences
Name the two outcomes, intoxication and sobriety
State what the chapter will establish

2.point: Among those who reached annihilation, the drunk (Bayazid, Hallaj) stayed in it and spoke of it; the sober (Junayd) returned, kept the secret in allusion, and went on to remaining.
steps: Bayazid reached annihilation and is the first named
In intoxication he spoke ecstatic sayings that sound like 'I am God'
The mystics read those sayings so that no man became God
Hallaj spoke openly and was not excused; the fault was the telling
Hence the sober spoke in allusion and kept the secret
Junayd kept the secret and uttered no ecstatic sayings
Junayd went further: beyond annihilation to remaining, while Bayazid stayed at the river
The sober return shows in ordinary duties kept (night prayer)
Conclusion

3.point: Ibn 'Arabi turned the sober's experience into the theory of the unity of being: one existence, creation its real manifestation, neither God nor apart from Him, and grasped only by experience.
steps: Ibn 'Arabi is the greatest heir
He named the theory: one existence, all else its manifestation
Where creation stands: nothing beside God, yet God is Manifest and Hidden, so what we see is His manifestation and not He
We are not God
Nor are we nothing: creation is real
The theory is above reason and known only by experience
Conclusion

4.point: The critics' three fears (insincerity, God merged with the world, law set aside) are answered by the masters' own words and lives; the only open question is whether Ibn 'Arabi was Shia, and his theory can be taken without settling it.
steps: Who the critics are and the three fears, plus a fourth for Shia readers
First fear answered: the 'urafa' erred but not in bad faith
Second fear answered: not pantheism (theory already showed creation is not God) and not indwelling (Tabataba'i, Amuli)
Third fear answered: intoxicated words are no rule, and the masters kept the law
Fourth concern stated: was Ibn 'Arabi Shia?
How the lectures meet it: experience cannot decide schools; visions follow prior theology; no one is taken wholesale
The evidence pulls both ways; the Sunni case is stronger; the theory can be taken without the loyalties
Conclusion

¶1.label: advance
¶1.why: Hook (the Sha'ban prayer) plus a one-line recall of Chapter Twelve; sets up the division the chapter is about.

¶2.label: advance
¶2.why: Names intoxication and sobriety and states what the chapter will establish; the opening's job.

¶3.label: advance
¶3.why: Supplies the first named figure who reached annihilation and ties his snake image to the false-self finding the section later relies on.

¶4.label: aside
¶4.why: How Bayazid got to annihilation (the four days of renunciation) and the Chapter Eleven cross-reference are not used by any later step; ¶5's 'a man so emptied' is only a verbal bridge. ¶3 already has him at annihilation.

¶5.label: advance
¶5.why: Supplies the step that the drunk spoke of what they saw: ecstatic sayings, and the saying that seems to claim 'I am God'.

¶6.label: advance
¶6.why: Raises the question the section must settle (can a believer say this?) and gives the first reading: God speaking from the tongue, as from the tree.

¶7.label: support
¶7.why: Completes the first reading with the lecture's gloss on the verse and the consequence that the words claim nothing for Bayazid, which ¶9 uses.

¶8.label: advance
¶8.why: Second reading, the one the mystics preferred: he spoke when removed from his own sight. ¶9's 'on either reading' needs it.

¶9.label: advance
¶9.why: Draws the conclusion from the two readings, that no man became God, which ¶11's 'the truth told' and Section 4's ¶32 depend on. Its middle sentence repeats ¶3 and ¶7.

¶10.label: advance
¶10.why: Hallaj, who was not excused; the charge was disclosure of secrets. Supplies the contrast the sober's secrecy turns on.

¶11.label: advance
¶11.why: Supplies the key step: the fault was the telling, so the sober spoke in allusion. The Abu Dharr tradition is its evidence.

¶12.label: advance
¶12.why: Names Junayd as the sober figure who kept the secret and uttered no ecstatic sayings. The death date, teachers, title and dress are padding around that one step.

¶13.label: advance
¶13.why: Supplies 'went further': intoxication is passing, remaining lies beyond annihilation.

¶14.label: advance
¶14.why: Supplies the step that Bayazid stopped (stayed in intoxication) while Junayd crossed; the explorer image carries it and ¶15 picks it up.

¶15.label: support
¶15.why: Evidence that the sober return shows in ordinary duties kept; ¶16 and ¶36 both use it.

¶16.label: restate
¶16.why: Summarises the section's steps already made. Only the last sentence (secret kept versus theory written) is new, and it is a bridge.

¶17.label: advance
¶17.why: Identifies Ibn 'Arabi as the heir and establishes his standing. The Chapter Five anecdote is a side remark inside an advancing paragraph.

¶18.label: advance
¶18.why: Names the theory and states its content: one existence, everything else its manifestation; he made a theory of what others alluded to.

¶19.label: advance
¶19.why: Puts the question where creation stands, reports 'nothing besides God', and brings in the verse that supplies Manifest and Hidden.

¶20.label: advance
¶20.why: Draws from the verse the double claim the point needs: what we see is His manifestation and is not He.

¶21.label: support
¶21.why: Frames the 'either God or nothing' dilemma that ¶22 answers and gives the lecture's words for the 'not God' half already stated in ¶20; ¶22's 'Nor' depends on it.

¶22.label: advance
¶22.why: Supplies the other half: creation is real, not illusion; a manifestation is not separate and still not He.

¶23.label: aside
¶23.why: A second authority (Imam 'Ali's oration) for the both-halves step that the verse and the lectures have already supplied; only ¶24 uses it, and ¶24 is itself a restatement.

¶24.label: restate
¶24.why: Its gloss repeats ¶20 and ¶22, and 'the sources state the truth, Ibn 'Arabi built the theory' repeats ¶18.

¶25.label: aside
¶25.why: A third voice (Khomeini's sea and waves) for a step already made twice, and it closes by saying the image does not hold. ¶26's 'does no better than the image' is only a verbal link.

¶26.label: advance
¶26.why: Supplies 'known by experience rather than argument' and resolves the secret-versus-theory puzzle left at ¶16.

¶27.label: support
¶27.why: An instance of experience matching the theory (Tabataba'i and Ibn 'Arabi) that grounds ¶26's step and that ¶28 and ¶29 generalise.

¶28.label: aside
¶28.why: A legacy note (Sadra, Khomeini, today's masters) that no step of the point uses; 'set the theory out in reasoned form' also sits awkwardly beside ¶26's 'above the rank of reason'.

¶29.label: restate
¶29.why: Summarises the section and bridges to the critics.

¶30.label: advance
¶30.why: Sets out who the critics are and reduces their complaints to the three fears, plus the fourth for Shia readers.

¶31.label: advance
¶31.why: Answers the first fear: errors possible, bad faith no, in Mutahhari's words.

¶32.label: advance
¶32.why: Splits the second fear into pantheism and indwelling and disposes of the first half by reference to Section 3.

¶33.label: advance
¶33.why: Answers the indwelling half with Tabataba'i and Amuli.

¶34.label: aside
¶34.why: Khomeini rebuking the accusers and the mystics who belittle jurists is a counter-charge, not an answer to the fear; no later sentence uses it.

¶35.label: advance
¶35.why: Third fear; supplies the first half of the answer: intoxicated words are no rule for a sober believer, and the claim that duties lift is unfounded.

¶36.label: advance
¶36.why: Second half of the answer: the masters' lives, drunk and sober, kept the law; ¶40 uses it.

¶37.label: advance
¶37.why: States the fourth concern and the evidence that Ibn 'Arabi may not have been Shia.

¶38.label: advance
¶38.why: The lectures' three ways of meeting the concern, including that no one is taken or rejected wholesale.

¶39.label: advance
¶39.why: Weighs the record, gives the honest verdict (Sunni case stronger), and draws the step the point ends on: the theory can be taken without the loyalties.

¶40.label: restate
¶40.why: Summarises the four answers and the chapter.

¶41.label: aside
¶41.why: Repeats ¶39's Gilani link and ends on a question the chapter does not answer; a hook for the next chapter, not a link in this one.
